learn.hook: Your phone may have chips from Taiwan, a screen from Korea and be assembled in Noida. No country makes everything alone.
points: Trade is the voluntary exchange of goods and services; two parties are required — one sells and the other buys — and it is mutually beneficial.
International trade is the exchange of goods and services among countries across national boundaries.
Countries trade to obtain commodities they cannot produce themselves, or that they can buy elsewhere at a lower price.
Trade encourages specialisation: each country produces what it is best at and exchanges the surplus.

example.q: India imports crude oil and exports software services. Explain why both countries involved benefit.
steps: India lacks enough crude oil, so it imports from oil-rich countries.
India has skilled IT workers, so it sells software services.
Each specialises in what it does best and gains from exchange.
example.answer: Both gain through specialisation and access to goods they lack

learn.reallife: India's top imports include crude oil, gold and electronics, while it exports refined petroleum, medicines, gems and IT services.

topics.title: History of trade: barter and money

learn.hook: Near Guwahati, every year after harvest, tribal communities still swap rice for fish and handicrafts — no money changes hands!
points: In early stages, trade was done through the barter system — direct exchange of goods without money.
Barter has difficulties: you must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have (double coincidence of wants); goods are hard to divide and value.

Every year after harvest, the Jon Beel Mela at Jagiroad, about 35 km from Guwahati (Assam), is possibly the only fair in India where barter is still alive; tribes and communities exchange their products.

The difficulties of barter were overcome by the introduction of money; earlier, rare objects with high intrinsic value — flintstones, cowrie shells, salt, peppercorns, cattle, copper, silver and gold — served as money.

example.q: A potter wants rice but the rice farmer wants fish. Why is barter hard here, and how does money help?
steps: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants — the farmer does not want pots.
The potter would have to find a third trader.
Money is accepted by all, so the potter sells pots for money and buys rice.
example.answer: Lack of double coincidence of wants; money is a common medium of exchange

learn.reallife: The Jon Beel Mela at Jagiroad (Assam) keeps alive India's barter tradition among Tiwa and other communities.

topics.title: History of trade: Silk Route, European commerce and slave trade

learn.hook: A bolt of Chinese silk once travelled 6,000 km on camel-back to reach a Roman senator's toga.
points: The Silk Route is an early example of long-distance trade, connecting Rome to China along about 6,000 km; traders carried Chinese silk, Roman wool, precious metals and other high-value goods via intermediate points in India, Persia and Central Asia.
After the disintegration of the Roman Empire, European commerce grew in the 12th and 13th centuries; with ocean-going warships, trade between Europe and Asia grew and the Americas were discovered.

From the 15th century, European colonialism began and a new, cruel form of trade emerged — the slave trade: the Portuguese, Dutch, Spaniards and British captured African natives and forcibly transported them to the Americas to labour on plantations.
The slave trade was a lucrative business for over two hundred years until it was abolished in Denmark (1792), Great Britain (1807) and the United States (1808).

example.q: Arrange the abolition of the slave trade by country in order of year.
steps: Denmark — 1792.
Great Britain — 1807.
United States — 1808.

learn.reallife: Indian merchants traded along the Silk Route through Taxila and Kashmir — pepper, cotton textiles and gems moved north while silk and horses came south.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

topics.title: Trade after the Industrial Revolution and the World Wars

learn.hook: In colonial times, India sent raw cotton to Manchester and bought back finished cloth — at a much higher price.
points: After the Industrial Revolution, demand for raw materials like grain, meat and wool expanded, but their monetary value fell relative to manufactured goods.

Industrialised nations imported primary products as raw materials and exported value-added finished products back to non-industrialised nations; in the later 19th century, industrial nations became each other's principal customers.
During World Wars I and II, countries imposed trade taxes and quantitative restrictions for the first time.
After the wars, organisations like the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), which later became the WTO, helped reduce tariffs.
The pattern of trade was shaped first by colonialism and later by globalisation.

example.q: Why did colonies lose out in the trade pattern after the Industrial Revolution?
steps: Colonies exported cheap raw materials.
They imported expensive manufactured goods.
Value addition (and profit) stayed in industrial nations.
example.answer: Raw materials lost value relative to manufactured goods, so colonies earned less

learn.reallife: Gandhiji's Swadeshi movement and khadi were a response to this unequal colonial trade pattern.

topics.title: Basis of trade: difference in national resources

learn.hook: Why does Australia sell wool, Malaysia sell rubber and Saudi Arabia sell oil? Look at their rocks and their weather.
points: The world's national resources are unevenly distributed because of differences in physical make-up — geology, relief, soil and climate.
Geological structure determines the mineral resource base; topographic differences ensure diversity of crops and animals — lowlands have more agricultural potential, while mountains attract tourists.
Mineral resources are unevenly distributed; availability of minerals provides the basis for industrial development.
Climate influences the type of flora and fauna in a region and so the products traded — wool comes from cold regions; bananas, rubber and cocoa grow only in tropical regions.

example.q: Explain how climate creates a basis for trade between Kerala and Kashmir.
steps: Kerala's tropical climate grows rubber, coconut, spices and bananas.
Kashmir's temperate climate grows apples, saffron and supports wool.
Each region trades its climate-specific products with the other.
example.answer: Different climates produce different goods, which are exchanged

learn.reallife: India exports iron ore from Odisha and Jharkhand but imports crude oil — a direct result of the uneven distribution of mineral resources.

topics.title: Basis of trade: population, development, investment and transport

learn.hook: Persian carpets, Chinese porcelain, Indonesian batik — some goods are traded because only one culture makes them so well.
points: Population factors: cultural factors give distinctive art and crafts valued worldwide — fine porcelain and brocades of China, carpets of Iran, leather work of North Africa and batik cloth of Indonesia.

Size of population: densely populated countries have large internal trade but little external trade, as most production is consumed locally; standard of living decides demand for better quality imported goods.

Stage of economic development: agriculturally important countries export agro products and import manufactured goods; industrialised nations export machinery and finished products and import food grains and raw materials.

Extent of foreign investment: it boosts trade in developing countries lacking capital for mining, oil drilling, heavy engineering, lumbering and plantations; industrial nations thereby secure food and minerals and create markets for their products.
Transport: lack of efficient transport once restricted trade to local areas; expansion of rail, ocean and air transport and better refrigeration and preservation have expanded trade spatially.

example.q: Why might a very populous country have relatively little external trade?
steps: Its large population consumes most of its agricultural and industrial output.
Internal markets absorb production.
So less is left for export.
example.answer: Most production is consumed in its large internal market

learn.reallife: Foreign investment in India's automobile sector (Hyundai, Suzuki) turned Chennai and Gujarat into export hubs for cars.

topics.title: Volume, composition and direction of trade

learn.hook: A tonne of microchips and a tonne of coal weigh the same — but their trade values are worlds apart. How do we measure trade?
points: Volume of trade: the actual tonnage of goods traded; since services cannot be measured in tonnes, the total value of goods and services traded is taken as the volume of trade.

Composition of trade: the nature of goods and services imported and exported. Primary products dominated early last century; manufactured goods later gained prominence; today manufacturing commands the bulk of trade but services (travel, transport, commercial services) show an upward trend.

Direction of trade: historically, present-day developing countries exported valuable goods and artefacts to Europe; in the 19th century the direction reversed, with Europe exporting manufactured goods for food and raw materials from colonies.

Europe and the USA emerged as major trade partners; Japan was the third. In the second half of the 20th century, Europe lost its colonies, and India, China and other developing countries began competing with developed countries.

example.q: India's exports shift from tea and jute (1950s) to software and medicines (today). Which aspect of trade has changed?
steps: The nature of goods exported changed.
That is the composition of trade.
It shows a shift from primary products to manufactures and services.

learn.reallife: India's software and services exports now rival its merchandise exports in value — a big change in composition.

topics.title: Balance of trade and balance of payments

learn.hook: If you spend ₹500 a month but earn only ₹300, your savings vanish. Countries face the same maths with imports and exports.
points: Balance of trade records the volume (value) of goods and services imported and exported by a country to other countries.
Balance of trade = value of exports − value of imports.
Positive or favourable balance: exports exceed imports. Negative or unfavourable balance: imports exceed exports.
A negative balance means the country spends more on buying goods than it earns by selling, which would ultimately exhaust its financial reserves.
Balance of payments is a broader record that also includes services, transfers and capital flows; both have serious implications for a country's economy.

example.q: Country X exports goods worth ₹450 crore and imports worth ₹600 crore. Find the balance of trade and state its type.
steps: Balance = exports − imports = 450 − 600.
= −150 crore.
Imports exceed exports → negative (unfavourable).

learn.reallife: India usually runs a merchandise trade deficit (large oil, gold and electronics imports) but a surplus in services trade from IT exports.

games.title: Favourable or unfavourable?
items: Spending more on buying than earning by selling
Earning more from sales abroad than spent on purchases

quiz.q: A country exports goods worth ₹1,200 crore and imports goods worth ₹900 crore. What is its balance of trade (in ₹ crore)?

topics.title: Types of trade, free trade and dumping

learn.hook: When cheap imported toys flooded Indian markets, local toy makers in Channapatna and Varanasi suffered. Is free trade always fair?
points: Bilateral trade: trade between two countries under an agreement to trade specified commodities.
Multilateral trade: trade with many countries at once; a country may grant 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) status to some partners.
Free trade or trade liberalisation: opening up economies for trade by lowering trade barriers like tariffs; goods and services from everywhere then compete with domestic products.
Globalisation with free trade can adversely affect developing countries if they are not given an equal playing field and unfavourable conditions are imposed.

Dumping: selling a commodity in two countries at prices that differ for reasons not related to costs — often selling abroad below cost or below the home price; free trade arrangements must protect countries from dumped goods, which can harm domestic producers.

example.q: India agrees with Sri Lanka to exchange tea machinery for spices only between the two. Separately, India trades with 150 countries under WTO rules. Classify.
steps: Two countries, specified goods → bilateral trade.
Many countries → multilateral trade.
example.answer: First is bilateral; second is multilateral

learn.reallife: India's Directorate General of Trade Remedies imposes anti-dumping duties, for example on certain cheap steel and chemical imports.

learn.hook: When two countries fight over steel tariffs, they don't go to war — they go to Geneva. That's where the WTO settles trade disputes.
points: In 1948, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was formed to free the world from high customs tariffs and other restrictions.
In 1994, members decided to set up a permanent institution for free and fair trade; GATT became the World Trade Organisation (WTO) from 1 January 1995. Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland.
The WTO is the only international organisation dealing with global rules of trade between nations; it sets the rules for the global trading system and resolves disputes between member nations.
It also covers trade in services such as telecommunication and banking, and issues like intellectual property rights.

Criticism: free trade does not make ordinary people more prosperous; it widens the gap between rich and poor; influential nations push their own interests; many developed countries have not fully opened markets to developing countries; health, workers' rights, child labour and environment are ignored. India is a founder member of the WTO.

example.q: How many years after GATT's formation did the WTO come into being?
steps: GATT formed in 1948.
WTO began on 1 January 1995.

learn.reallife: India has used WTO dispute settlement in cases on agricultural subsidies and steel duties, and defends food security stockholding at WTO meetings.

topics.title: Regional trade blocs: ASEAN, CIS and EU

learn.hook: A Belgian truck drives into France and Germany without stopping for customs and pays in euros everywhere. That's the power of a trade bloc.
points: Regional trade blocs encourage trade between countries with geographical proximity, similarity and complementarity in trading items, and curb restrictions on trade of the developing world.
Today about 120 regional trade blocs generate 52 per cent of world trade.

ASEAN (Association of South-East Asian Nations): headquarters Jakarta, Indonesia; formed August 1967; members include Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia; trades agro products, rubber, palm oil, rice, copra, coffee, minerals (copper, coal, nickel, tungsten), petroleum and natural gas, software products.
CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States): headquarters Minsk, Belarus; formed in 1991 by former Soviet republics; trades crude oil, natural gas, gold, cotton, fibre and aluminium.

EU (European Union): headquarters Brussels, Belgium; began as the European Economic Community in March 1957, became the EU in February 1992; single market with a common currency (euro); trades agro products, minerals, chemicals, wood, paper, transport vehicles, optical instruments, clocks, works of art and antiques.

example.q: Match each bloc to its headquarters: ASEAN, CIS, EU.
steps: ASEAN → Jakarta (Indonesia).
CIS → Minsk (Belarus).
EU → Brussels (Belgium).

learn.reallife: India's Act East Policy and the ASEAN–India Free Trade Area link Indian trade closely with ASEAN; India–EU FTA talks are also under way.

topics.title: Regional trade blocs: LAIA, NAFTA, OPEC and SAFTA

learn.hook: A small group of oil-exporting countries meeting in Vienna can change petrol prices in Patna. Meet OPEC.
points: LAIA (Latin American Integration Association): headquarters Montevideo, Uruguay; originated in 1960; members include Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela.

NAFTA (North American Free Trade Agreement): USA, Canada and Mexico; came into force in 1994; trades agro products, motor vehicles, automotive parts, computers and textiles. It was replaced by the USMCA in 2020.

OPEC (Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries): headquarters Vienna, Austria; members include Algeria, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Libya, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Venezuela; the main commodity is crude petroleum.

SAFTA (South Asian Free Trade Agreement): members are the SAARC countries — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka (Afghanistan joined later); came into effect in January 2006; aims to reduce tariffs on intra-regional trade.
Exam tip: learn the table of blocs — headquarters, members, year of origin and commodities.

learn.hook: Cheaper imported phones are great — until local factories shut, forests are cleared for export crops, and fish stocks crash. Trade has two faces.
points: International trade is mutually beneficial if it leads to regional specialisation, higher production, better standard of living, worldwide availability of goods, equalisation of prices and wages, and diffusion of knowledge and culture.
It can be detrimental if it leads to dependence on other countries, uneven levels of development, exploitation, and commercial rivalry leading to wars.

Global trade affects the environment, health and well-being: as countries compete to trade more, production and use of natural resources spiral up, and resources get used faster than they can be replenished — marine life depletes, forests are cut, river basins are sold to private water companies.

Multinational corporations in oil, gas, mining, pharmaceuticals and agri-business may expand at all costs, creating pollution; if only profit matters and environmental and health concerns are ignored, there can be serious future implications.
While goods and capital move freely under globalisation, the movement of people (labour) across borders remains restricted.

example.q: Sort these effects of trade: higher production, dependence on imports, diffusion of knowledge, commercial rivalry.
steps: Beneficial: higher production, diffusion of knowledge.
Detrimental: dependence on imports, commercial rivalry leading to conflict.

learn.hook: Ships too big to reach Athens dock at Piraeus instead. Ports come in many types — and each has a job.
points: Ports and harbours are the chief gateways of international trade, providing docking, loading, unloading and storage; the importance of a port is judged by the size of cargo and number of ships handled, and its cargo indicates the development of its hinterland.

By cargo: industrial ports specialise in bulk cargo (grain, sugar, ore, oil, chemicals); commercial ports handle general cargo (packaged and manufactured goods) and passengers; comprehensive ports handle bulk and general cargo in large volumes — most great world ports.

By location: inland ports lie away from the coast, linked to the sea by a river or canal (Manchester by canal, Memphis on the Mississippi, Mannheim and Duisburg on the Rhine, Kolkata on the Hooghly); out ports are deep-water ports built away from the main port to serve it — Piraeus for Athens.

By function: oil ports (tanker ports like Maracaibo in Venezuela, Esskhira in Tunisia, Tripoli in Lebanon; refinery port Abadan on the Persian Gulf); ports of call on main sea routes for refuelling, water and food (Aden, Honolulu, Singapore); packet stations or ferry ports for passengers and mail over short distances, in facing pairs (Dover and Calais across the English Channel).

Entrepot ports are collection centres for goods brought from different countries for re-export (Singapore for Asia, Rotterdam for Europe, Copenhagen for the Baltic); naval ports serve warships (Kochi and Karwar in India).

steps: (a) On the Hooghly, away from the sea → inland port.
(b) Deep-water port serving Athens → out port.
(c) Ferry port facing Calais → packet station.
(d) Serves warships → naval port.
example.answer: (a) inland, (b) out port, (c) packet station, (d) naval port

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
